issues.legal_issue: A reviewing court may decide the representative status of a body when the pleadings and responses squarely put that status in dispute, even if the appeal was framed more narrowly.
material_facts: The original petitioners claimed to act as administrators or representatives of a religious endowment and sought relief concerning its management.
The respondents expressly disputed the representative body’s authority to represent the deity and to claim a role in managing the institution.
The disputed status had been raised in the pleadings and proceedings before the appellate court.
issues.conclusion: The appellate court was entitled, and in the circumstances required, to decide the representative body’s locus or status; the challenge to its doing so was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: In the court’s full writ jurisdiction, a serious dispute about the petitioners’ asserted authority or status cannot be ignored when it arises from the pleadings and is expressly contested. The court distinguished public-interest litigation from proceedings in which petitioners assert personal rights as administrators or representatives. No earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.

rule.if: representative_status_disputed and (status_claimed_in_pleadings or relief_sought_as_representative) and writ_proceeding

predicates.representative_status_disputed: The opposing parties expressly denied that the claimant body had authority to represent the institution or claim a role in its management.
predicates.status_claimed_in_pleadings: The petitioners asserted in their pleadings that they held an administrative or representative status.
predicates.relief_sought_as_representative: The petitioners sought relief on the basis that they represented an institution or its beneficiaries.
predicates.writ_proceeding: The dispute came before the court in a writ proceeding.

issues.definition: When a representative claim is made in a writ proceeding and the opposing parties dispute it, the court may decide that status.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory committee created to oversee institutional annuity and its accounting does not thereby acquire general management powers over the institution.
material_facts: The governing statute principally dealt with acquisition of institutional land and payment of annuity to the institution’s head.
The amendment creating the committee described its functions as control over annuity utilization and verification of proper maintenance.
The amendment’s stated purposes included control over annuity and verification and audit of accounts.
The existing customary managers’ powers had not been removed by the statute.
issues.conclusion: The committee’s role is limited to control and verification concerning annuity and other government grants under the statute, including the accounting of their use; it does not manage or oversee the institution’s secular or religious affairs.
issues.legal_principle: The court interpreted Section 25A in the context of the Act as a whole, including the definition of the institution’s head in Section 2(d), the annuity provisions in Section 8(5), and the amendment’s objects and reasons. The words concerning proper maintenance refer to verification of accounts relating to annuity and grants, not general management. No earlier case was necessary to this interpretation.

predicates.statutory_committee_created: A law created a committee for a religious or charitable institution.
predicates.committee_purpose_limited_to_funding_ove: The law’s text and stated purposes confine the committee to oversight of specified institutional funds and their accounting.
predicates.customary_managers_not_displaced: The governing law did not remove the existing managers or transfer general management to the committee.

issues.definition: A committee created for limited funding oversight has only that role when the law does not displace the institution’s existing managers.

issues.legal_issue: Established customary managers retain their customary authority to elect their representatives and manage an institution when no valid law has displaced that authority.
material_facts: Historical judicial decisions recognized the principal priest families as trustees and the elected head priests as their agents or managers.
The established practice was that the principal priest families elected the head priests, who managed the institution’s religious and secular affairs.
The customary election practice continued, and the claimed later change to a broader management arrangement was unsupported by acceptable evidence and lacked acceptance by the customary body.
The statute creating a limited funding-oversight committee did not transfer general management powers or abolish the customary rights.
A separate proceeding seeking broader relief against the customary managers was pending.
issues.conclusion: The customary body retained its right to elect the head priests and their customary authority over religious and secular management; the asserted management regulation could not deprive it of those rights. The court left the pending separate proceeding unaffected.
issues.legal_principle: The court relied on the prior civil-court determination of the customary trusteeship and election practice, the Calcutta High Court decision in Baroda Kanta v. Bangshi Nath, AIR 1940 Cal. 269, and earlier judicial findings concerning the customary authority of the priest families. It held that the land-acquisition statute and its limited committee provision had not displaced those customary rights. The court did not determine the merits of the separate proceeding under Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

rule.if: customary_management_dispute and customary_rights_judicially_recognized and customary_practice_continued and not valid_law_displacing_custom

predicates.customary_management_dispute: The proceeding concerned who could elect the institution’s managers and manage its affairs.
predicates.customary_rights_judicially_recognized: Earlier judicial decisions recognized the relevant group’s customary trusteeship or election rights.
predicates.customary_practice_continued: The group continued to elect the managers under the established practice, and no accepted evidence showed that the practice had ended.
predicates.valid_law_displacing_custom: A valid law transferred or abolished the customary management authority.

issues.definition: Where courts have recognized a continuing customary management right and no valid law displaces it, the customary managers retain their election and management authority.

issues.legal_issue: Election rules may distinguish between the customary managerial group and other devotees when allocating committee election rights, and statutory wording referring to alternative groups does not require both groups to participate in every institution.
material_facts: The rules provided for a secretary elected by the traditional managerial group and for other committee members elected by a wider group of devotees.
The traditional group had a distinct, historically recognized role in managing the temple, while other priests and worshippers were included among devotees for the wider election.
The rules did not bar female members of the traditional group from inclusion in the electoral roll; the State accepted that their claims for inclusion could be considered.
The petitioners did not establish that the other priest group had the same institutional status as the traditional managerial group.
The State framed rules for the particular institution, and the legislature did not modify them after they were laid before it.
issues.conclusion: The rules were valid and did not violate equality or conflict with the statute. The statutory reference to the two groups permits election by either group, depending on which group manages the particular institution; the traditional group could elect the secretary, while devotees could elect the other committee members.
issues.legal_principle: The court read Section 25A, including its reference to the two groups separated by a slash, in the context of the Act’s institution-specific scheme. It relied on Section 30, which authorizes rules, and treated the unmodified rules as explaining and supplementing the Act. The distinct customary status of the traditional group justified the different electoral colleges; the wider devotee electorate provided participation for others. The court found no Article 14 discrimination on the facts.

predicates.rules_for_single_institution: The rules establish an election arrangement for a particular religious or charitable institution.
predicates.traditional_group_has_distinct_managemen: A customary group has a distinct and established role in managing that institution.
predicates.other_interested_persons_included_in_wid: Other priests, worshippers, or interested persons are included in a broader electorate for other committee positions.
predicates.female_members_not_excluded: The rules do not exclude female members of the customary group from the relevant electoral roll.

issues.definition: An institution may reserve one committee election to its distinct customary management group while allowing a wider group to elect other members, provided the rules do not exclude women from the customary group.

issues.legal_issue: A claim that a private religious custom violates equality cannot succeed where the claimed equality is not established on the evidence, and judicial decisions made in a judicial capacity are not State action under the constitutional definition of the State.
material_facts: The petitioners challenged the customary restriction of the head-priest election to male members of the principal priest families and sought to include women and other priests.

The parties disputed the women’s participation, expertise, and qualifications in the institution’s religious and secular affairs, and the record contained no authoritative textual or other material resolving that dispute.
The petitioners did not establish that the other priest group was equally situated, and did not explain why the claimed extension should be limited to the groups they identified.
The custom was not created by State action, and no State law regulating the relevant management practice had been enacted.
The challenge sought judicial relief against a private customary practice.
issues.conclusion: The court denied relief because the claimed equality was not established on the record. It held that Article 13(1) does not invalidate religious customs and personal laws protected by Articles 25 and 26, and that courts acting judicially are not the State under Article 12.
issues.legal_principle: The court applied Articles 12, 13, 14, 25, and 26. It distinguished Sant Ram v. Labh Singh, Bhau Ram v. B. Baijnath Singh, and Atam Prakash v. State of Haryana, which concerned pre-emption rights, and relied on the harmonious reading of Articles 25 and 26 discussed in The Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Mutt and Shri Venkataramana Devaru v. State of Mysore. It also discussed Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala, Pannalal Bansilal Pitti v. State of Andhra Pradesh, and Seshammal v. State of Tamil Nadu concerning religious freedom and state regulation. On the meaning of the State, it relied on Pradeep Kumar Biswas v. Indian Institute of Chemical Biology, Naresh Shridhar Mirajkar v. State of Maharashtra, Triveniben v. State of Gujarat, and Poonam v. Sumit Tanwar. The court held that judicial acts are not State action, although courts may fall within the definition when acting administratively.

rule.if: private_custom_equality_challenge and (equality_not_established_on_evidence or no_state_action_creating_custom) and judicial_relief_sought

predicates.private_custom_equality_challenge: A party challenges a private religious or customary practice as discriminatory.
predicates.equality_not_established_on_evidence: The evidence does not establish that the excluded persons are equally situated or qualified for the claimed participation.
predicates.no_state_action_creating_custom: The challenged practice was not created by governmental action or by a law regulating that practice.
predicates.judicial_relief_sought: The party asks a court to invalidate or alter the private practice through judicial proceedings.

issues.definition: A private-custom equality challenge is dismissed when equality is not established or the custom is not attributable to State action and the requested relief is judicial.

issues.legal_issue: A court acting on its judicial side is not the State for purposes of a claim that it must apply fundamental rights directly against private parties.
material_facts: The petitioners argued that the judiciary became the State when hearing a dispute and therefore had to prevent a private custom from continuing.
The challenged custom arose between private parties, without relevant executive or legislative action.
The requested relief would have required the court to treat the private dispute itself as State action merely because it was adjudicated in court.
issues.conclusion: The judiciary is not the State when performing judicial functions; courts may fall within the definition of the State when acting in an administrative capacity, such as in matters concerning their employees.
issues.legal_principle: The court interpreted Article 12 contextually and held that judicial decisions cannot be subjected to writ jurisdiction as State action merely because a court hears a case. It relied on Pradeep Kumar Biswas v. Indian Institute of Chemical Biology, Naresh Shridhar Mirajkar v. State of Maharashtra, Triveniben v. State of Gujarat, and Poonam v. Sumit Tanwar. It distinguished judicial functions from administrative actions by courts.

predicates.fundamental_right_claim_against_private_: A party invokes a fundamental right to challenge conduct by a private person or group.
predicates.court_acting_judicially: The court is performing an adjudicative function rather than an administrative function.

issues.definition: When a court adjudicates a fundamental-rights claim against a private party, its judicial act does not itself make the court the State.
